claim: Innate pluripotency of mouse embryos transits from naive to primed state as the inner cell mass differentiates into epiblast.
source: Innate pluripotency of mouse embryos transits from naive to primed state as the inner cell mass differentiates into epiblast.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mouse embryo development in the abstract.

claim: In vitro counterparts of naive and primed states are embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and epiblast stem cells (EpiSCs), respectively.
source: In vitro, their counterparts are embryonic (ESCs) and epiblast stem cells (EpiSCs), respectively.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about in vitro cell types corresponding to developmental states.

claim: Activation of the FGF signaling cascade results in mouse ESCs differentiating into mEpiSCs.
source: Activation of the FGF signaling cascade results in mouse ESCs differentiating into mEpiSCs, indicative of its requirement in the shift between these states.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about FGF signaling's role in mouse ESC differentiation.

claim: Only mouse ESCs correspond to the naive state among mammalian ESCs.
source: However, only mouse ESCs correspond to the naive state; ESCs from other mammals and from chick show primed state characteristics.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the uniqueness of mouse ESCs.

claim: ESCs from other mammals and from chick show primed state characteristics.
source: However, only mouse ESCs correspond to the naive state; ESCs from other mammals and from chick show primed state characteristics.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ESCs from non-mouse species.

claim: The finch blastoderm has mESC-like properties.
source: The finch blastoderm has mESC-like properties, while chick blastoderm exhibits EpiSC features.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental characterization.

claim: Chick blastoderm exhibits EpiSC features.
source: The finch blastoderm has mESC-like properties, while chick blastoderm exhibits EpiSC features.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental characterization.

claim: In the absence of FGF signaling, finch cells retained expression of pluripotent markers.
source: In the absence of FGF signaling, finch cells retained expression of pluripotent markers, which were lost in cells from chick or aged finch epiblasts.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from cell culture experiments.

claim: Pluripotent markers were lost in cells from chick or aged finch epiblasts in the absence of FGF signaling.
source: In the absence of FGF signaling, finch cells retained expression of pluripotent markers, which were lost in cells from chick or aged finch epiblasts.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from cell culture experiments.

claim: The naive state of pluripotency is evolutionarily conserved among amniotes.
source: Our data suggest that the naive state of pluripotency is evolutionarily conserved among amniotes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from the experimental data comparing finch and chick embryos.

claim: Mouse ESCs are at naive state.
source: In the mouse, ESCs are at naive state (Nichols and Smith, 2009), which recent evidence suggests is most similar to cells from embryonic day (E) 4–4.5 of mouse development (Boroviak et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The naive state in mouse is most similar to cells from embryonic day (E) 4–4.5 of mouse development.
source: In the mouse, ESCs are at naive state (Nichols and Smith, 2009), which recent evidence suggests is most similar to cells from embryonic day (E) 4–4.5 of mouse development (Boroviak et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boroviak et al., 2014.

claim: Cells from E4-4.5 mouse embryos can give rise to derivatives of all three germ layers as well as germ cells.
source: Cells taken from this stage can give rise to derivatives of all three germ layers as well as germ cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mouse embryonic cells.

claim: Naive state cells express genes associated with pluripotency such as Oct3/4 (Pou5f1), Sox2, and Nanog.
source: These cells, both in their native naive state and in culture, express genes associated with pluripotency such as Oct3/4 (Pou5f1), Sox2, and Nanog (2).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about pluripotency markers.

claim: Mouse ESCs can be propagated while maintaining expression of pluripotency markers using defined media that includes an inhibitor of FGF signaling or its downstream Erk/MAP kinase transduction pathway.
source: Using defined media that includes the presence of either an inhibitor of FGF signaling or its downstream Erk/MAP kinase transduction pathway, mouse ESCs (mESCs) can be propagated while maintaining the expression of these pluripotency markers (Ying et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ying et al., 2008.

claim: Mouse epiblast stem cells (mEpiSCs) are derived from embryos at E5.5 and are in the primed state.
source: A second pluripotent cell type in the mouse, epiblast stem cells (mEpiSCs), is derived from embryos that are later in development (E5.5) and is in what has been termed, the primed state (Brons et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brons et al., 2007.

claim: mEpiSCs have a more limited potency than mESCs.
source: These cells have a more limited potency and require different culture condition for in vitro propagation (Lanner and Rossant, 2010), with a dependency on FGF-mediated ERK activation for the maintenance of pluripotent gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lanner and Rossant, 2010.

claim: mEpiSCs require FGF-mediated ERK activation for the maintenance of pluripotent gene expression.
source: These cells have a more limited potency and require different culture condition for in vitro propagation (Lanner and Rossant, 2010), with a dependency on FGF-mediated ERK activation for the maintenance of pluripotent gene expression.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mEpiSCs.

claim: Pluripotent ESCs from human share the requirement for ERK signaling with mEpiSCs.
source: Pluripotent ESCs from other mammalian organisms, such as human (Thomson et al., 1998; Schatten et al., 2005), and from non-mammalian amniotes, such as chick (Pain et al., 1996), share this requirement for ERK signaling (Tesar et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Thomson et al., 1998; Schatten et al., 2005; and Tesar et al., 2007.

claim: Pluripotent ESCs from chick share the requirement for ERK signaling with mEpiSCs.
source: Pluripotent ESCs from other mammalian organisms, such as human (Thomson et al., 1998; Schatten et al., 2005), and from non-mammalian amniotes, such as chick (Pain et al., 1996), share this requirement for ERK signaling (Tesar et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pain et al., 1996 and Tesar et al., 2007.

claim: The primed state of pluripotency is evolutionarily conserved in mammalian and non-mammalian amniotes.
source: Hence, the primed state of pluripotency is evolutionarily conserved in mammalian and non-mammalian amniotes.
evidence: This is inferred from the shared requirement for ERK signaling across species.

claim: The naive state has so far only been confirmed in the mouse and rat.
source: However, the naive state has so far only been confirmed in the mouse (Ying et al., 2008) and rat (Buehr et al., 2008; Li et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2013b), raising the possibility that this state is not conserved among the amniotes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on mouse and rat.

claim: Recent reports suggest that with specific reprogramming factors and culture conditions a naive state may also exist for human ESCs.
source: More recent reports suggested that with specific reprogramming factors and culture conditions such a naive state may also exist for human ESCs, although the exact nature of these naive-type human cells is under debate (Takashima et al., 2014; Theunissen et al., 2014; Ware et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: The exact nature of naive-type human cells is under debate.
source: More recent reports suggested that with specific reprogramming factors and culture conditions such a naive state may also exist for human ESCs, although the exact nature of these naive-type human cells is under debate (Takashima et al., 2014; Theunissen et al., 2014; Ware et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations indicating ongoing scientific debate.

claim: Avian species share key molecular and cellular features of epiblast morphogenesis with mammals.
source: These include avian species, which share key molecular and cellular features of epiblast morphogenesis with the mammals (Sheng, 2014), yet are evolutionarily distant enough to serve as an outgroup.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sheng, 2014.

claim: Fertilization of avian oocytes takes place internally.
source: As in all amniotes, fertilization of avian oocytes takes place internally and avian embryos undergo some development prior to egg-laying (oviposition).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about avian reproduction.

claim: Avian embryos undergo some development prior to egg-laying (oviposition).
source: As in all amniotes, fertilization of avian oocytes takes place internally and avian embryos undergo some development prior to egg-laying (oviposition).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about avian development.

claim: Chicken embryos at oviposition are already at a late blastula/early gastrulation stage (EGK stage X).
source: However, chicken embryos at oviposition are already at a late blastula/early gastrulation stage (Eyal-Giladi and Kochav (EGK) stage X) (Eyal-Giladi and Kochav, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eyal-Giladi and Kochav, 1976.

claim: Chicken embryos at oviposition have a columnar epithelialized epiblast overlying scattered hypoblasts.
source: These embryos have a columnar epithelialized epiblast overlying scattered hypoblasts and are thus morphologically similar to E5.5 mouse embryo, later than the stage at which mESCs can be derived.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about chicken embryo morphology.

claim: Chicken embryos at oviposition are morphologically similar to E5.5 mouse embryo.
source: These embryos have a columnar epithelialized epiblast overlying scattered hypoblasts and are thus morphologically similar to E5.5 mouse embryo, later than the stage at which mESCs can be derived.
evidence: This is an inference based on morphological comparison.

claim: Chicken embryos at oviposition are at a stage later than the stage at which mESCs can be derived.
source: These embryos have a columnar epithelialized epiblast overlying scattered hypoblasts and are thus morphologically similar to E5.5 mouse embryo, later than the stage at which mESCs can be derived.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison to E5.5 mouse embryo.

claim: Japanese quail embryos are laid at a stage later than chicken embryos.
source: The Japanese quail embryos are laid at a stage later than the chicken embryos (Sellier et al., 2006), while the ovipositional stage of zebra finch embryos is unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sellier et al., 2006.

claim: The ovipositional stage of zebra finch embryos was unclear prior to this study.
source: The Japanese quail embryos are laid at a stage later than the chicken embryos (Sellier et al., 2006), while the ovipositional stage of zebra finch embryos is unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Early-staged avian embryos can generate cells that show some characteristics of mammalian ES cells after introduction of reprogramming factors.
source: Early-staged avian embryos can generate cells that show some of the characteristics of mammalian ES cells (Jean et al., 2015) after the introduction of reprogramming factors (Rossello et al., 2013; Dai et al., 2014) or after the manipulation of culture conditions (Pain et al., 1996; Jean et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Early-staged avian embryos can generate cells that show some characteristics of mammalian ES cells after manipulation of culture conditions.
source: Early-staged avian embryos can generate cells that show some of the characteristics of mammalian ES cells (Jean et al., 2015) after the introduction of reprogramming factors (Rossello et al., 2013; Dai et al., 2014) or after the manipulation of culture conditions (Pain et al., 1996; Jean et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Zebra finches are a model system commonly used in neurobiological studies of social behavior.
source: The finches are a model system commonly used in neurobiological studies of social behavior (Brazas and Shimizu, 2002; Svec et al., 2009), vocalization, and learning (Jarvis, 2004; Petkov and Jarvis, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using finches.

claim: Zebra finches are used in studies of vocalization and learning.
source: The finches are a model system commonly used in neurobiological studies of social behavior (Brazas and Shimizu, 2002; Svec et al., 2009), vocalization, and learning (Jarvis, 2004; Petkov and Jarvis, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using finches.

claim: The finch genome has been sequenced.
source: In addition, the finch genome has been sequenced (Warren et al., 2010) and their relatively small adult body sizes (4–7 times smaller than adult chickens) and shorter generation time (2–3 months for finches vs 4–6 months for the chickens) makes it feasible to breed them within a normal laboratory setting.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Warren et al., 2010.

claim: Adult finches are 4–7 times smaller than adult chickens.
source: In addition, the finch genome has been sequenced (Warren et al., 2010) and their relatively small adult body sizes (4–7 times smaller than adult chickens) and shorter generation time (2–3 months for finches vs 4–6 months for the chickens) makes it feasible to breed them within a normal laboratory setting.
evidence: This is stated as factual information about finch size.

claim: Finches have a generation time of 2–3 months.
source: In addition, the finch genome has been sequenced (Warren et al., 2010) and their relatively small adult body sizes (4–7 times smaller than adult chickens) and shorter generation time (2–3 months for finches vs 4–6 months for the chickens) makes it feasible to breed them within a normal laboratory setting.
evidence: This is stated as factual information about finch reproduction.

claim: Chickens have a generation time of 4–6 months.
source: In addition, the finch genome has been sequenced (Warren et al., 2010) and their relatively small adult body sizes (4–7 times smaller than adult chickens) and shorter generation time (2–3 months for finches vs 4–6 months for the chickens) makes it feasible to breed them within a normal laboratory setting.
evidence: This is stated as factual information about chicken reproduction.

claim: Finch embryos are laid at stage EGK-VI to EGK-VIII.
source: Our results suggested that finch embryos are laid at stage EGK-VI to EGK-VIII, much earlier than the chicken embryos, and are morphologically more similar to the E4–E4.5 mouse embryos from which mESCs can be derived.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on morphological characterization.

claim: Finch embryos at oviposition are morphologically more similar to E4–E4.5 mouse embryos from which mESCs can be derived.
source: Our results suggested that finch embryos are laid at stage EGK-VI to EGK-VIII, much earlier than the chicken embryos, and are morphologically more similar to the E4–E4.5 mouse embryos from which mESCs can be derived.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on morphological comparison.

claim: Cells derived from finch blastoderm at oviposition and cultured in the presence of a MEK inhibitor and LIF retained expression of Nanog.
source: Cells derived from the finch blastoderm at oviposition and cultured in the presence of a MEK inhibitor and Leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF) retained expression of the pluripotent markers; Nanog, PouV expression, and alkaline phosphatase (AP) activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on cell culture experiments.

claim: Cells derived from finch blastoderm at oviposition and cultured in the presence of a MEK inhibitor and LIF retained PouV expression.
source: Cells derived from the finch blastoderm at oviposition and cultured in the presence of a MEK inhibitor and Leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF) retained expression of the pluripotent markers; Nanog, PouV expression, and alkaline phosphatase (AP) activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on cell culture experiments.

claim: Cells derived from finch blastoderm at oviposition and cultured in the presence of a MEK inhibitor and LIF retained alkaline phosphatase (AP) activity.
source: Cells derived from the finch blastoderm at oviposition and cultured in the presence of a MEK inhibitor and Leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF) retained expression of the pluripotent markers; Nanog, PouV expression, and alkaline phosphatase (AP) activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on cell culture experiments.

claim: Chicken cells taken from newly laid embryos and cultured under the same conditions did not produce Nanog-positive aggregates.
source: In contrast, chicken cells taken from newly laid embryos and cultured under the same conditions did not produce Nanog, PouV, or AP-positive aggregates.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on cell culture experiments.

claim: Chicken cells taken from newly laid embryos and cultured under the same conditions did not produce PouV-positive aggregates.
source: In contrast, chicken cells taken from newly laid embryos and cultured under the same conditions did not produce Nanog, PouV, or AP-positive aggregates.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on cell culture experiments.

claim: Chicken cells taken from newly laid embryos and cultured under the same conditions did not produce AP-positive aggregates.
source: In contrast, chicken cells taken from newly laid embryos and cultured under the same conditions did not produce Nanog, PouV, or AP-positive aggregates.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on cell culture experiments.

claim: Birds and mammals share a common regulatory mechanism in the maintenance of pluripotency.
source: Our data suggest that birds and mammals share a common regulatory mechanism in the maintenance of pluripotency.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: Finch eggs are laid in intervals of between 20 and 29 hr.
source: Finch eggs are laid in intervals of between 20 and 29 hr, with most laid following a 24- to 25-hr periodicity.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Most finch eggs are laid following a 24- to 25-hr periodicity.
source: Finch eggs are laid in intervals of between 20 and 29 hr, with most laid following a 24- to 25-hr periodicity.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Approximately 10% of finch eggs at oviposition are at EGK-VI.
source: Based on the EGK staging system for pre-oviposition chick embryos (Eyal-Giladi and Kochav, 1976), we found that finch embryos from newly laid eggs ranged from EGK-VI to EGK-VIII, with ∼10% of eggs at EGK-VI and the rest at EGK-VII and -VIII.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study.

claim: The rest of finch eggs at oviposition (approximately 90%) are at EGK-VII and -VIII.
source: Based on the EGK staging system for pre-oviposition chick embryos (Eyal-Giladi and Kochav, 1976), we found that finch embryos from newly laid eggs ranged from EGK-VI to EGK-VIII, with ∼10% of eggs at EGK-VI and the rest at EGK-VII and -VIII.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study.

claim: At EGK-VI, the finch embryo is composed of similar-sized blastoderm cells organized into 7–8 layers.
source: At EGK-VI (early blastula), the embryo was composed of similar-sized blastoderm cells organized into 7–8 layers (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a morphological observation supported by Figure 1A.

claim: The subgerminal (blastocoel) cavity was not as apparent in finch embryos at EGK-VI as in similarly staged chick embryos.
source: The subgerminal (blastocoel) cavity was not as apparent as in similarly staged chick embryos (Eyal-Giladi and Kochav, 1976; Sheng, 2014).
evidence: This is a comparative observation with citation to chick embryo descriptions.

claim: By EGK-VIII, the subgerminal cavity and the area pellucida became apparent in finch embryos.
source: By EGK-VIII (mid-blastula stage) (Figure 1B), the subgerminal cavity and the area pellucida became apparent and the embryo was thinner at the center of the blastoderm (4–5 cell-thick) than at EGK-VI.
evidence: This is a morphological observation supported by Figure 1B.

claim: At EGK-VIII, the finch embryo is 4–5 cells thick at the center of the blastoderm.
source: By EGK-VIII (mid-blastula stage) (Figure 1B), the subgerminal cavity and the area pellucida became apparent and the embryo was thinner at the center of the blastoderm (4–5 cell-thick) than at EGK-VI.
evidence: This is a morphological observation supported by Figure 1B.

claim: At EGK-VIII, cells located apically in finch embryos (putative epiblast precursors) are smaller than those located closer to the yolk side (putative hypoblast precursors).
source: Cells located apically, closer to the vitelline membrane (the putative epiblast precursors) were smaller than those located closer to the yolk side (the putative hypoblast precursors).
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the study.

claim: A low level of Hhex expression was detected in the hypoblast precursors at EGK-VIII in finch embryos.
source: A low level of Hhex expression was detected in the hypoblast precursors.
evidence: This is a molecular observation from in situ hybridization.

claim: Post-ovipositional incubation of around 6 hr yielded finch embryos at EGK-X.
source: Post-ovipositional incubation of around 6 hr yielded finch embryos at EGK-X (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: At EGK-X, the epiblast and hypoblast are clearly separated in finch embryos.
source: At this stage, the epiblast and hypoblast were clearly separated and the epiblast showed a columnar epithelial organization.
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the study.

claim: At EGK-X, the epiblast shows a columnar epithelial organization in finch embryos.
source: At this stage, the epiblast and hypoblast were clearly separated and the epiblast showed a columnar epithelial organization.
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the study.

claim: Strong Hhex expression was detected in the hypoblasts at EGK-X in finch embryos.
source: In addition, strong Hhex expression was detected in the hypoblasts.
evidence: This is a molecular observation from in situ hybridization.

claim: Hhex is a marker for endoderm cells.
source: To probe morphological and molecular heterogeneity of the finch blastoderm, we first used section analysis of embryos stained for Hhex, a marker for endoderm cells (Thomas et al., 1998) (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thomas et al., 1998.

claim: At EGK-VI, most of the finch blastodermal cells express E-cadherin but appear unpolarized.
source: At EGK-VI, most of the blastodermal cells appear unpolarized, however, express E-cadherin (D).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At EGK-VII, the finch blastoderm does not show any columnar cells typical of epithelial organization.
source: At EGK-VII, while thinner, the blastoderm does not show any columnar cells typical of epithelial organization (E).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining shown in Figure 1E.

claim: At EGK-X, clear epithelial organization can be visualized in finch embryos with polarized E-cadherin.
source: At EGK-X, clear epithelial organization can be visualized, with polarized E-cadherin and morphological segregation in the bright-field image (F).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining shown in Figure 1F.

claim: At EGK-VI, both E-cadherin and ß-catenin are expressed in all cells of the finch blastoderm.
source: At EGK-VI, both E-cadherin (Figure 1D) and ß-catenin (Figure 1G) were expressed in all cells.
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining shown in Figures 1D and 1G.

claim: At EGK-VI, E-cadherin and ß-catenin staining in finch embryos does not appear to be enriched in any particular region of the cell.
source: Staining did not appear to be enriched in any particular region of the cell and epithelialization was not apparent.
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining.

claim: Epithelialization is not apparent at EGK-VI in finch embryos.
source: Staining did not appear to be enriched in any particular region of the cell and epithelialization was not apparent.
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining.

claim: By EGK-VIII, formation of an epithelial cell-sheet is not observed in finch embryos.
source: By EGK-VIII, formation of an epithelial cell-sheet was not observed although the nuclei of the outermost, putative epiblast, cells appeared more regularly organized (Figure 1E,H).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining shown in Figures 1E and 1H.

claim: By EGK-VIII, the nuclei of the outermost, putative epiblast, cells in finch embryos appear more regularly organized.
source: By EGK-VIII, formation of an epithelial cell-sheet was not observed although the nuclei of the outermost, putative epiblast, cells appeared more regularly organized (Figure 1E,H).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining shown in Figures 1E and 1H.

claim: By EGK-VIII, deep, putative hypoblast, cells in finch embryos appear to down-regulate both E-cadherin and ß-catenin.
source: In contrast, deep, putative hypoblast, cells appeared to down-regulate both proteins.
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining.

claim: By EGK-X, E-cadherin is up-regulated in the lateral regions of the epiblast cells in finch embryos.
source: By EGK-X, E-cadherin was up-regulated in the lateral regions of the epiblast cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining shown in Figure 1F.

claim: At EGK-X, finch epiblast cells form a discrete columnar cell-sheet.
source: Their epithelial morphology was further evidenced by formation of a discrete columnar cell-sheet.
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the study.

claim: Chick embryos at oviposition are more similar to the finch embryo after incubation.
source: Analysis of chick embryos at oviposition revealed that it was more similar to the finch embryo after incubation (Figure 1I), sharing features with the finch late blastula (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by Figures 1I and 1J.

claim: Chick embryos at oviposition share features with the finch late blastula.
source: Analysis of chick embryos at oviposition revealed that it was more similar to the finch embryo after incubation (Figure 1I), sharing features with the finch late blastula (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by Figures 1I and 1J.

claim: The early blastoderm consists of cells fated to become the epiblast and hypoblast as well as germ cells.
source: The early blastoderm consists of cells fated to become the epiblast and hypoblast as well as germ cells (Eyal-Giladi et al., 1981; Hatada and Stern, 1994; Lawson and Schoenwolf, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In chick, the germ cell fate is marked by immunoreactivity to SSEA-1 and EMA-1 antibodies.
source: In chick, the germ cell fate is marked by immunoreactivity to the stage-specific embryonic antigen 1 (SSEA-1) and epithelial membrane antigen 1 (EMA-1) antibodies (Jung et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jung et al., 2005.

claim: In finch embryos, SSEA-1 and EMA-1 immunoreactivity is observed predominantly in the epiblast precursor.
source: In finch embryos, immunoreactivity of these proteins were observed predominantly in the epiblast precursor (Figure 2A,B,E–H), with SSEA-1 staining being stronger than EMA-1.
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining shown in Figure 2.

claim: SSEA-1 staining is stronger than EMA-1 in finch embryos.
source: In finch embryos, immunoreactivity of these proteins were observed predominantly in the epiblast precursor (Figure 2A,B,E–H), with SSEA-1 staining being stronger than EMA-1.
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining shown in Figure 2.

claim: Few hypoblast precursor cells in finch embryos are positive for SSEA-1 and EMA-1.
source: Few hypoblast precursor cells were positive for these markers (Figure 2C,D,E–H).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining shown in Figure 2.

claim: In mouse embryos, Gata4 expression marks the specification of the hypoblast/primitive endoderm.
source: In mouse embryos, Gata4 expression marks the specification of the hypoblast/primitive endoderm (Soudais et al., 1995) and the SoxB family member, Sox2 expression marks the epiblast precursors (Avilion et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Soudais et al., 1995 and Avilion et al., 2003.

claim: In mouse embryos, Sox2 expression marks the epiblast precursors.
source: In mouse embryos, Gata4 expression marks the specification of the hypoblast/primitive endoderm (Soudais et al., 1995) and the SoxB family member, Sox2 expression marks the epiblast precursors (Avilion et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Avilion et al., 2003.

claim: In chick, Sox3 is expressed in epiblast precursors.
source: In chick, a different SoxB family member, Sox3 is expressed in epiblast precursors (Rex et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rex et al., 1997.

claim: Sox3 and Gata4 can be detected at finch oviposition.
source: Both immunostaining and in situ hybridization confirmed that Sox3 and Gata4 could be detected at finch oviposition and that lineage segregation between these two cell types could be distinguished (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining and in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2.

claim: Lineage segregation between Sox3 and Gata4 expressing cells can be distinguished at finch oviposition.
source: Both immunostaining and in situ hybridization confirmed that Sox3 and Gata4 could be detected at finch oviposition and that lineage segregation between these two cell types could be distinguished (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining and in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2.

claim: Sox3 is more abundant in the cells at the vitelline membrane side in finch embryos at oviposition.
source: Sox3 was more abundant in the cells at the vitelline membrane side (Figure 2I,K) and Gata4 more abundant in the yolk side (Figure 2J,M).
evidence: This is an observation from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2.

claim: Gata4 is more abundant in the yolk side in finch embryos at oviposition.
source: Sox3 was more abundant in the cells at the vitelline membrane side (Figure 2I,K) and Gata4 more abundant in the yolk side (Figure 2J,M).
evidence: This is an observation from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2.

claim: In mouse, both Gata6 and Sox17 mark all of endodermal lineages.
source: In mouse, both Gata6 and Sox17 mark all of endodermal lineages (Fujikura et al., 2002; Kanai-Azuma et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fujikura et al., 2002 and Kanai-Azuma et al., 2002.

claim: Sox17 is expressed in the hypoblast in the finch blastoderm from oviposition.
source: Sox17 was expressed in the hypoblast in the finch blastoderm from oviposition, with some positive cells also detected in the epiblasts (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is an observation from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Some Sox17 positive cells are also detected in the epiblasts of finch embryos at oviposition.
source: Sox17 was expressed in the hypoblast in the finch blastoderm from oviposition, with some positive cells also detected in the epiblasts (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is an observation from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Sox17 expression is similar at EGK-IX/X in finch embryos as at oviposition.
source: Expression was similar after epithelization at EGK-IX/X (Figure 2M).
evidence: This is an observation from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2M.

claim: Gata6 expression is restricted to the hypoblast lineage at EGK-VII/VIII in finch embryos.
source: Gata6 expression was restricted to the hypoblast lineage (Figure 2O) at EGK-VII/VIII, which is more apparent by EGK-X (Figure 2P).
evidence: This is an observation from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2O.
